title: BridgeKit first-hit playbook notes
content:
Goal: create a tiny, opinionated "first-hit" experience for new integrators that gets a working sample app and telemetry in under 12 minutes. This doc is a sprint-era sketch: concrete steps, pain points from last user test, and a short experiment plan.

Audience: backend engineers and platform integrators who want a reproducible path to a minimal production-like integration (auth, simple retry, basic cost telemetry). Not a full tutorial — focus on the first successful run and the smallest set of follow-ups.

What success looks like (metrics to validate):
- Time-to-first-success: median <= 12 minutes in usability tests (n=10)
- First-call success rate: >90% (includes getting credentials + sample request)
- Telemetry ingestion: events for token_count + latency appear in console within 30s of first call
- Follow-through: 40% of testers complete the short feedback task (rate prompt vs cost)

Top-level flow (minimal):
1) Create API key (link) — quick note on scopes and safety
2) Clone tiny sample: bridgekit-starter (git clone URL)
3) Run single command to bootstrap local env (one-liner: curl | sh style) — sets env vars, installs deps
4) Start sample server and run one SDK call (sync or streaming) to get a reply
5) Check Console for telemetry + cost breakdown
6) Toggle fallback to smaller model (one checkbox) and re-run to observe stable degrade

Detailed steps (what to ship in the quickstart folder):
- README.md: 5 short sections, no more than 300 words total (Problem, What you’ll run, One-liner, What you should see, Next steps)
- bootstrap.sh: idempotent, prompts for API key if env var absent, simple OS detection (mac/linux), installs py/ts sample
- sample/ (single-file examples): node index.js and python main.py — both run the same small prompt and print a compact JSON with latency and token counts
- network-sim: script to simulate 50ms/200ms latency for local dev testing (tiny proxy wrapper)
- smoke-check: script that verifies Console events via the ingestion API and prints PASS/FAIL

UX decisions / anti-patterns to avoid:
- Avoid large example apps. Keep sample app <= 150 LOC in primary file.
- No multi-repo onboarding. Everything upfront in a single tarball or monorepo subfolder.
- Explicitly call out common error messages and one-line fixes (bad key, network blocked, rate-limited).

Checklist for doc authors (this doc is for the writer and the reviewer):
- [ ] One-liner bootstrap works on a fresh VM image (tested in CI)
- [ ] README uses nontechnical copy for concept explanation, then short commands for devs
- [ ] Console screenshot flow updated to match current UI (update date stamp in image alt text)
- [ ] Telemetry keys used in sample are ephemeral and scrubbed in repo history
- [ ] Local smoke-check returns PASS in <15s for healthy infra

Known rough edges from first round of user tests (observations):
- New testers paused when asked to set PROJECT_ID vs API_KEY — ambiguity on where to paste keys. Action: change prompt to only require API_KEY and auto-derive names.
- Some Windows users hit permission issues with bootstrap script. Action: add Windows zip path and Powershell snippet in README.
- Testers expected an observable cost estimate before the call. Action: display a tiny pre-call estimate based on token heuristics (example shown in preflight).

Quick troubleshooting snippets to include in docs (copyable lines):
- If you see 401: export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk_live_xxx  # make sure no trailing whitespace
- If network fails: curl -v https://api.redwood.example/v1/ping  # check DNS & firewall
- If telemetry missing: ./smoke-check --verbose  # shows ingestion logs and sample events

Experiment plan (A/B candidates):
- A: One-liner bootstrap (curl|sh) vs B: guided interactive wizard (node CLI that prompts) — measure completion time and drop-off
- A: Show pre-call cost estimate inline vs B: only post-call cost report — measure confidence + follow-up actions
- A: Include streaming example in first flow vs B: defer streaming to "next steps" — measure confusion & errors

Session script for a 20-minute workshop (for field/solutions teams):
- 0–3m: 1-slide micro-intro (what BridgeKit unlocks)
- 3–6m: Run bootstrap one-liner together
- 6–12m: Execute sample request, show Console telemetry and cost panel
- 12–16m: Toggle fallback to smaller model and re-run
- 16–20m: Quick feedback + next steps (invite to sandbox slack channel)

Open questions (to resolve before finalizing quickstart):
- Should bootstrap create a sandbox project automatically or require manual project creation? (security + billing tradeoffs)
- For pre-call cost estimate: what default token pricing should we show for hosted users? (engineering to propose number)
- Do we expose a tiny server-side helper to validate API key live (it would simplify UX but adds backend surface area)?

Task owner map (short):
- bootstrap script & one-liner: Jonah Lee (owner) — due: 2025-11-07
- README and screenshots: Priya Singh (owner) — due: 2025-11-14
- Smoke-check + CI job: Diego Alvarez (owner) — due: 2025-11-21
- Usability test recruiting & run: Maya Patel (owner) — schedule for 2025-12-02

Notes to self / rough copy fragments (to iterate into formal README):
- "Run the one-liner, post a snippet in #bridgekit-sandbox, we’ll RT and help debug."
- "This sample intentionally uses a small prompt and deterministic settings so first results are repeatable."
- "If you want to try streaming, switch to stream mode with --stream and watch the same output in ~real-time."

Small appendix examples (short):
- Minimal Node request (pseudo):
  const { Client } = require('@redwood/bridgekit');
  const c = Client({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY });
  const r = await c.generate({ model: 'rwd-small-1', prompt: 'Summarize: \"Ship it\"' });
  console.log(JSON.stringify({ text: r.text, tokens: r.tokens, latency_ms: r.latency }));

- Smoke-check expected JSON event (single-line):
  {"event":"sample_request","latency_ms":"<number>","tokens":"<number>","project":"bridgekit-demo"}

Next milestone: convert this to a tidy README + bootstrap.sh and run the first CI build that publishes the tarball. Ship candidate to field for 2nd round of quick user tests by 2025-12-08.

-- end of notes --
